meta.title: yellow-agents — an AI playing Pokémon Yellow

hero.title: An AI that plays Pokémon Yellow by reading the game's memory
hero.lead: The game runs in a Game Boy emulator inside Python. The code reads the RAM and hands the AI a summary of the game: where it is, the party, the text on screen. The AI only decides which buttons to press. This page shows how each part works, with real data from every session.
hero.caption: Baseline recorded frame by frame: from a new game to receiving Pikachu, with player CLAUDE and rival GEMINI. A fixed script plays here, not the AI: it is the yardstick every agent will be compared against.

how.title: How it works
how.lead: Each layer does one thing. Whatever is mechanical stays in code; the model only comes in where there is a decision.

layers.name: Emulator
layers.text: Headless PyBoy at full speed. Presses buttons, saves and loads the game. One direction press walks exactly one tile.

layers.name: State
layers.text: Reads RAM through the pret/pokeyellow symbols and builds a JSON: map, position, party, battle and what is written on screen.

layers.name: MCP tools
layers.text: The actions any MCP client (Claude Code, Codex…) can call. Every input is validated before it touches the game.

layers.name: Recording
layers.text: Every run becomes a JSONL with state, action and screenshot. That is where this page's data comes from.

layers.name: Models
layers.text: One interface for Claude, OpenAI and local models (Ollama).

layers.name: Agent
layers.text: Planner, navigation and battle, with memory and routing between a local model and Claude.

how.principle: Project rule: walking, reading memory and timing buttons are deterministic code, never a prompt. The model decides strategy, goals and battles.

phase1.title: Giving the AI eyes and hands

walk.title: One press, one tile
walk.problem: The tool promises that one direction press walks one tile. Holding the button for a fixed time, the player sometimes didn't move. No timing combination got all 8 moves right.
walk.how: A step takes 16 to 18 frames, and the game only reads a new direction between steps. Now the code watches RAM: it holds the direction until the step counter (wWalkCounter) starts, releases, and waits for it to reach zero. If the map changed (door, stairs), it waits for the transition to finish.
walk.decision: Closed loop on RAM instead of fixed timing (ADR 0001). Benchmarks count emulator frames, not presses.
walk.legend: Each square is one press: 1 = walked one tile, 0 = didn't move. On the closed-loop route: {moved} moved, {blocked} hit a wall (as expected) and {warped} changed map.

decoder.title: From RAM to the state the AI reads
decoder.problem: Sending screenshots to the model is expensive, slow and imprecise. The model also needs to know whether a dialogue is open or a menu is waiting for an answer.
decoder.how: Real memory bytes, exported from a run. Each highlighted field becomes a key in the JSON the AI receives. The screen (wTileMap) is a 20×18 grid of tile codes; letters use the game's own charmap, so the text comes straight from RAM.
decoder.decision: State comes from RAM, with addresses taken only from pret's symbol file. Screenshots are for when you need to see where things are on the map.

mcp.title: One MCP call, step by step
mcp.problem: Any AI client must be able to play, and a model makes mistakes: it may send a button that doesn't exist or a dangerous file name.
mcp.how: A real session recorded over stdio: the client calls the tool, the server validates the input, the emulator runs the frames and the state comes back. An invalid input stops at the server and the error message reaches the model.
mcp.decision: Expected errors use ToolError, so the model sees the reason. Before, it only got "Error executing tool".

note.new_game: powers on, goes through the intro and types the name CLAUDE (the rival stays GEMINI).
note.press_buttons: three presses, three tiles: from (3,6) to (1,5).
note.screenshot: a picture of the screen, without advancing a single game frame.
note.error: invalid button: the server rejects it before touching the emulator and explains why.

baseline.title: Baseline: a script to Pikachu
baseline.lead: The project's metric is emulator frames to each milestone: deterministic, independent of the machine and the model. This is the result of a fixed script with no AI at all. Every agent will be compared against it.

journal.title: Project journal
journal.lead: Each work session records its goal, problems (symptom → cause → solution → evidence), decisions and numbers. Dead ends count too.
journal.ptOnly: The journal is written in Portuguese, the project's working language.

footer.rom: No ROM is distributed: the project runs on the user's own dump. Pokémon is a trademark of Nintendo, Creatures and GAME FREAK; this is a non-commercial study project.
